utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Mladic, conversations -- loud conversations with security is not what you're expected to do. Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The next witness to be called, we'll hear his testimony through videolink. Let's first establish whether the videolink is functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you wait for a second --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Do you hear --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I hereby confirm that we hear you and we can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you we can see you as well. The witness is present in the room where you are. Could you tell us who else are present.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, apart from the witness and myself, there is ITSS official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar, at the other side of the videolink. Could the witness please stand so that he can make a solemn declaration. If he is able to stand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text, as we see, has been handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blagojevic. Please be seated. Mr. Blagojevic, if, for whatever reasons, you would need a break, don't hesitate to ask me. You'll now first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you please tell us your full name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Nedo Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D1719.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the first page of this document, there's a signature. Can you identify whose signature we see here.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please turn to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On the last page, we also see a signature. Can you tell us whose signature this is?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Again, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now the indicate that is recorded here, does it -- is it in accord with your recollection of the date when you would have signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the right date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, after signing this statement, did you have occasion to read the same in the Serbian language during our proofing session to check to see if everything is correctly recorded in it?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it, and it's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you today questions based on the same topics as in your written statement, would your answers, in substance, be the same?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, since you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth, does that mean, then, that everything that is contained in your statement is truthful?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would tender the statement 1D1719 as a public exhibit. There's also one associated document which is 65 ter number 05636 which we would also tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, first the document, the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The statement receives D878, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. And the associated exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives Exhibit Number D879, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also admitted into evidence. And that was the 65 ter number as you mentioned it, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, I would read the public witness summary of the statement. The witness joined the VRS in May of 1992. He was a communications officer that served as chief of communications for the Drina Corps from 1 November 1992 through the end of the war, and, indeed, until he was retired in 1997. He started as a major and attained the rank of colonel in 1995. For reasons of safety and security, at the beginning of the operation in Srebrenica, the witnesses installed KZU-61 devices at the RRU-1 at Pribicevac to protect conversations from being intercepted. He personally installed KZU-63 devices on the RUP-12 devices being used by units involved in the operation for the same purpose. He likewise proposed that all combat activities be communicated by way of encrypted written documents and it was done accordingly. The frequencies used by the VRS did not change during the war as there was no reason for that. These frequencies are reflected in the associate exhibit which has now received the number D879. That completes the public summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. If you have any further questions you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to turn to page 4 in your statement in both languages and focus on paragraph 21 briefly. In this paragraph, you talk about the installation of some KZU-61 and KZU-63 devices at the beginning of the operation in Srebrenica. First of all, can you clarify for us what Srebrenica operation is at issue, whether by name or by date?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but the operation was called Krivaja, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know the year?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The year was 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Next, sir, I would like to ask you: The acronym KZU, what does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: KZU means encryption device.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to ask you about these devices, both the KZU-61 and the KZU-63. Could you please explain for us how those devices functioned and what kind of radio communications did they affect?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: KZU-61 was for the protection of speech on one line, one segment. KZU-61 is a device that I installed on a relay device called RRU-1, whereas KZU-63 also serves for the protection of speech and it's mounted on RRU-12.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, how do these devices protect speech communications? How do they function?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: KZU-61 and KZU-63 scramble speech to such an extent that you can't listen to it without a special device.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, you say in your statement that you personally installed the KZU-63 on the RUP-12 radios that the units involved in the Srebrenica operation utilized. Could someone from the ABiH with the same type of radio install a KZU-63 device and just turn on their radio and automatically intercept the scrambled signal from these devices, or was something else required?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Just plugging in an encryption device does not in itself imply confidentiality. You also have to put in the code for the key, and these keys inside the device ensure the confidentiality of speech. Without inserting the key in the encryption device, the encryption device on its own is useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this key that you're talking is it -- how is it input?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Manually, using a keyboard. On the device itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the RUP-12 that you discuss, was that a simplex or a duplex radio system?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: RUP-12 is a simplex communication. I speak, you listen, and then vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, prior to 1995, prior to this point in 1995, had you assisted in the setting up of any other encryption devices at Pribicevac, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When the Tactical Group Pribicevac was established and a command post was put in place in Pribicevac, we also installed the encryption device KZU-31. It is a device for the encryption of written communication, of text, for purposes of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 22, which is at -- on the same page in the Serbian and starts on the bottom of the same page in English and flows onto the next page, here you are talking of how you asked for an order to be issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- I see that you now are leaving outside the technicalities of paragraph 21 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, Witness, you are recorded as having referred to RRU-12, whereas in your statement, and later by Mr. Ivetic, reference was made to RUP-12. Did you intend to refer do anything else than the RUP-12?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said RRU-12? I don't think I mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then where I take it where the transcript reads "RRU-12," that we have to understand it as "RUP-12." As far as the code is concerned, I think that you mainly explained that the code was needed for encryption. If such radio signals would be intercepted, would you need to have the same code apart from the encryption devices, but would you need the same code in order to understand what was said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. The same device, the same code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 22, you are talking of how you asked for an order to be issued that all communication as to combat activities be transmitted by a written document. Can you tell us when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That order that I wrote, I wrote it in the beginning of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir --

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: And it was signed by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said I wrote the order in December 1992. It was signed by the corps commander, and it was to the effect that all communications regarding combat activities had to be encrypted and sent in writing because it was possible. We had encryption devices for speech and for written information, and I insisted that it be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to move to a different topic to discuss the RRU-800 radio relay device. First of all, sir, how old were the RRU-800 radio relay devices that were in use in the communications system of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: RRU-800 were old, even when I was at the academy, 1965, 1966, and 1967 [as interpreted]. And in 1995 especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to these RRU-800 radio relay devices at the VRS, would you describe the power usage of these machines, that is, could they operate at 100 per cent of their original power output?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Considering that these devices were old, the useful range for acceptable communication, in terms of speech or written information, was 25 per cent of the original range because it was obsolete.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, were there any other situations when these RRU-800 radio relay devices would be purposefully operated at less than full power?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood the question correctly, no, such situations didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just for my understanding, the whole issue of the -- of the power and the use and all being old, is that to be found somewhere in the statement or is it in addition to what -- I mean, I see the 800 in paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's all in addition to the statement, Your Honours, supplementing the tactical details that were mentioned in -- I believe actually earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I also remember well that this was a hot issue when we heard evidence by the Prosecution on the use of this? Then I'm a bit surprised at what then turned out to be a real matter of dispute, that that is not dealt with in this statement because that's what I would expect then to focus on. Because that's my recollection that we had a lot of questions about that, especially by the Defence. So I was wondering why it doesn't appear here now, if that was one of the hot items.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I am thinking the same thing, but, of course, I also remembered this and was expecting to hear it as we're hearing it now. So we're not surprised but we would have preferred it to be, of course, in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, for the Chamber as well, we have not studied the radio systems in detail. But I remember that, that was one of the items. But it is clear now to me that I didn't miss anything in the statement. It's in addition to what we find in the statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I would also actually bring to the attention -- Your Honour referenced paragraph 16 and then I just turned to the prior paragraphs and I see the English translation has RRU-880 instead of 800 for paragraphs 8 and 12 which I did not note previously. I -- I don't know if I have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have it in paragraph 8, we have the 880. We have --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it in 12. Yes. Perhaps you clarify with the witness whether in his statement -- if the original gives only one number, only 800 and not 880, then we need a new translation. If, however, the original also has various numbers, then we should clarify with the witness whether these are the same or different --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Looking at the Serbian original I only see RRU-800 and the other two devices that are identified, so it looks like a scrivener's error in the English translation. So we'll have to upload a corrected version of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, does --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You agree with that. Then let's have a new translation rather than to spend more time on it now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'd like to look at paragraph 10 and 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do, I just have a little clarification here to ask. Sir, at page 9, line 4 of today's transcript, when you were first asked about the RRU-800 you are recorded as having said: "RRU-800 were old even when I was at the academy, 1965, 1966 and 1967." Were you at the academy in those years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how this was interpreted to you. What I said was 1975, 1976, and 1977. Not 1965 but 1975.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That clarifies my problem. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at page 3 in both versions, I'd like to look at paragraphs 10 and 12. First of all, sir, you identify the RUP-12 as supporting circular communication in all horizontal directions; whereas you say the RRU-800 is uni-directional. What is the difference in layman's terms for these two types of communication?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: A RUP-12 is a radio device. Its antenna broadcasts a signal within a circle of 360 degrees, whereas the radio relay device and its antenna direct impasses in one direction, not 360 degrees. Just one direction, one degree. This is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then for the purposes of locating and receiving that signal on the other end, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The same device has to exist on the other side, and the antennas have to face each other in order to enable communication. I'm talking about a radio relay device. When it comes to a radio device, the situation is entirely different. Those devices can be scattered all over the area in a circle of 360 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, based upon your experience and in your opinion, could the radio axes from Zvornik towards the VRS Main Staff be intercepted by enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, from Zvornik towards the Main Staff, i.e., the corps command, because Zvornik was subordinated to the corps, of course, not to the Main Staff. But we used the relay hub of the Main Staff in Veliki Zep. It was not a radio approach but a radio relay approach. A radio relay station in Zvornik could not be intercepted by Muslim forces because the radio relay station was in the Drina valley and some 200 metres behind it there was a natural obstacle, a slope, which was about 100 to 150 metres above the radio relay station. It was towering over it, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, this was not in the statement, this specific comment about the inability to intercept. And this is not in prior testimony either.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is. It is in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It -- this kind of information needs to be in statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it in the statement, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is not in the statement otherwise I would have directed to the statement. It is in the Popovic transcript which is where I got it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If he could point that out, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can get that at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey, then we'll see that after the next break. I would have one question for the witness in this context. Witness, you explained to us the difference between the radio relay and radio. Radio being circular, 360 degrees. May I take it that for radio relay, that at least there is a small range in which direction the signals will be sent? I can imagine that it is 3 degrees or 5 degrees. Could you tell us anything about how broad that signal is transmitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In degree terms, up to 1 degree, at the most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For example --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly switch off all the unnecessary microphones, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One degree is the breadth of the signal at some 10 to 15 kilometres distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which requires a very precise direction of the signal in order not to miss the receiver, relay receiver station. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, now I want to look at the associated exhibit mentioned in paragraph 25; that is, D879. If we can call up the same in e-court, and I believe you have a copy there at your location. First of all, sir, I note there are some handwritten entries. Can you tell us who generated these handwritten notations we see?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: These handwritten entries were done by me personally in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were these handwritten notations communicated to the recipient of this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is actually my report to the chief of communications of the Main Staff where I communicate the real frequencies in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is dated 2nd October 1993. What can you tell us about the frequencies that were in use by the VRS for the same radio relay points prior to this date?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: These are the frequencies of the Drina Corps. I don't know why the chief of communications of the Main Staff asked for this. Perhaps he did not have all the necessary data in order to avoid any overlapping and scrambling --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The connection was bad and the interpreter missed one part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, as a result of that, I communicated to him a the overview of the frequencies that were being used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the interpreter did not catch your entire answer. Could you please continue from where you told us that you did not have all the necessary data in order to avoid any overlapping and scrambling. Could you continue your answer from that point on.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of communications of the Main Staff was a -- communicated this information on the current frequencies which were in use at the time. This was supposed to help him with further planning. This helped him to work normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if someone is receiving a signal from an RRU-800 transmission, how many frequencies should be recorded for receipt of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As you can see in the document, the radio relay device has two frequencies: One for transmission; one for receipt. We are talking about RRU-800.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in paragraph 24, if we can return to your statement which now has the number D878, and it is on page 5 in both languages. In paragraph 24 --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That should be the next page in the ... there we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 24, you say there was no reason to change the frequencies. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: What I meant was that it was impossible to communicate normally on those frequencies for either technical reasons or because of weather conditions or scrambling. Those were the main reasons why frequencies needed to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did those reasons exist on the VRS side during the war such that the frequencies needed to be changed?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no such reasons. Hence, there were no frequency changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you also say here in this paragraph that you did not have the right or power to change these frequencies. What entity or entities would have had to have been involved in ordering a change in the frequencies used by the VRS radio relay system?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Radio relay communications of the Main Staff and the Drina Corps relied on the radio relay communications of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Therefore, the communications organs of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were involved in the planning and organisation of radio relay communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, could the VRS unilaterally change their -- their radio relay frequencies without the Yugoslavian authorities being involved in the same?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The chief of communications of the Main Staff and I, as the chief the communications of the Drina Corps, were in a position to change frequencies. However, our devices were directed towards the devices of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia which means that we would have been automatically cut off from communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, my last question for you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before do you that, just for my better understanding. In relation to the last answer, sir, you said that would mean "that we would have been automatically cut off from communication." Why that? The communication between the Drina Corps and the Main Staff, would that be cut off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that would have been cut off because our hubs and the devices of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were our mediators for communication. They were in between, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about the communication between the Drina Corps and subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you have a schematic of the relay communications of the Drina Corps, if you had it you would see that the Drina Corps, when it comes to the RRU-800 device, to communicate with any brigade we had to go through the hub of the Main Staff and relay hub of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, my last question. Police units and authorities, did they utilize the -- this same VRS radio system that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Police units had their own system and that was mostly a radio system. I did not hear the rest of your question. You mentioned the police, but you also mentioned some other body. What was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I only asked about the police units and police authorities.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then, Colonel, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my direct examination. And I will get that transcript reference to Mr. McCloskey as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did I also -- looking at the 65 ter summary, it doesn't say anything about impossibility of interceptions, whereas that seems to be the clue of much of the witness -- of this witness's evidence. But I just check that and I don't see any such observation mentioned in the 65 ter summary. Before, Mr. McCloskey, I give you an opportunity to -- to start your cross-examination, I would have one question for the witness. Witness, police units and police authorities, how did they communicate with the VRS staff, VRS Main Staff, Corps Staff, whatever. How did they communicate with the military structures with which they co-operated or operated its -- I leave it in that respect as open as possible. How did they communicate with the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Police units and police authorities communicated with the command of the Drina Corps and its units either directly in immediate contacts or by telephone. Sometimes they used our military communications in order to establish a contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm looking at the clock. Mr. McCloskey, we could do two things: Either start now, if would you have a seven-minutes first portion to deal with, or take an early break and then resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If could I start now and try to respond to that one point that the witness just made regarding Zvornik and interceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Blagojevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, you just said on temporary transcript page 12, line 18, that the -- and I quote: "Radio relay station in Zvornik could not be intercepted by Muslim forces because the radio relay station was in the Drina valley and some 200 metres behind it there was a natural obstacle, a slope, which was about 100 to 150 metres above the radio relay station." Now, to communicate to or from Zvornik, you would go from this Zvornik hub you're talking about to the radio relay station in Serbia called Gucevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And from the radio relay station Gucevo in Serbia, the next link in the chain was to another radio relay station in Serbia called Cer; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you testified as a Defence witness for Vujadin Popovic many years ago; I believe it was 2006. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And let me remind you of something you testified to in Popovic. I take it you testified in Popovic truthfully?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this testimony can be found on page 36 -- it's 65 ter 31884, page 36 in e-court. It was at page 22296, lines 1 through 6 in the Popovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, in part, you say: "And as for Vlasenica-Veliki Zep, Cer-Gucevo and Gucevo-Zvornik, this is where it was possible to listen in under the condition that you enter the radio relay beam which was difficult because we applied measures of anti-electronic protection. You could only intercept oral communication, which was impossible with the written communication because the written communication was always encrypted ..." Sir, here, you say twice that it would be possible to intercept along this path to Zvornik. You say it's difficult, but you said that if it entered the radio beam, it can be intercepted. So which is correct: Popovic back then or what you've just said to Mr. Ivetic today?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Both things are correct. Mr. Ivetic asked me about the interception of conversations from Zvornik. As for the interception of conversations taking place in Zvornik, since the antenna was directed towards Gucevo, i.e., eastwards, and the Muslim forces and their interception devices were westwards. On top of that, from the Zvornik radio device, towards Muslim forces there was a natural obstacle and it was impossible to intercept conversations. When it comes to Gucevo, Vlasenica, Veliki Zep and Cer and from the direction of Gucevo which sent a beam westwards from the station towards the Muslim forces, there it was possible to intercept a signal and to record a conversation taking place but only in that direction, from Gucevo in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But all conversations from Zvornik had to go through the radio relay hub Gucevo-Cer, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's where the Muslims, even in your own testimony, could intercept?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. From Zvornik towards Gucevo the radio relay device sent a signal on transmission frequency which was then forwarded so it could not be intercepted at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't say Zvornik. I said Gucevo-Cer.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: That applies to Gucevo-Cer as well. Muslims could not intercepted those conversations because the axis is Zvornik-Gucevo-Cer and they could not intercept any of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me remind you what you said in Popovic one more and that you also told us today that it was true. "And as for Vlasenica-Veliki Zep, Cer-Gucevo, and Gucevo-Zvornik, this is where it was possible to listen in under the condition that you enter the radio relay beam which was difficult because we applied measures of anti-electronic protection. You could only intercept oral communications ..." Is that a true statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand by what I said and I re-confirm this. You quoted the axis well, Vlasenica-Veliki Zep, Cer-Zvornik, but this is a direction, and from that direction conversations could be intercepted. However, when it comes to Zvornik, Gucevo, Cer and further on, that direction could not be intercepted because we're talking about two different frequencies, the transmission frequency on the one hand and the receipt frequency on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They're both RRU-800, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you cannot protect RRU-800's speech, could you?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Speech on RRU-800 cannot be protected as a group. Particular, separate channels can be protected on different frequencies --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter missed the last bit of the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, lastly, you mentioned a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- could we hear the last part of the answer which the interpreters missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel, I think you're going to have to repeat your last answer, if you can, because we weren't able to interpret all of it.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: A speech on RRU-800 could be protected with KZU-61 devices, but only on separate channels on devices with such frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Lastly, before the break, you mentioned a diagram.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if it may be helpful, I would ask us to go to 65 ter 31858.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I won't ask you any questions about this, but perhaps you could take a look at it at the break in case it will be helpful in answering questions. This is -- it should be for an Operation Stit 1995 that you developed the comms plan for, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be page 25 in the English; page 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will leave it at that, since it's break time. Though we can point out -- we can see Cer in the right-hand corner of this, going over to Gucevo, going over to the first Zpbr, the Zvornik Brigade. And these are the relay routes we have been talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness take his time over the break to check that because it might be difficult for him to immediately check every detail of what is presented to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then before we take that break -- Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. First of all, to correct, it's the 2008 Popovic transcript, not 2006. The transcript reference I was relying up is transcript page 22295, line 19, through 22296, 6. And one last point, Your Honours, I received the cross documents but a lot of the English translations are denied access in e-court. If we can perhaps meet over the break to try to get that resolved so we can get access to all the documents, that would be appreciated. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that it will be investigated why the English is not accessible. Witness, before we take the break, I would have -- I seek one clarification. When we started with the possibilities of intercepting radio relay communication from Zvornik, you explained to us that it was impossible to intercept those because -- well, to say it short, because of the terrain not being accessible to the Muslims and the terrain obstructing intercept from a different direction. Now, later, you were asked about the later portions of the trajectory the radio signals would travel and then you said, yes, Vlasenica, Veliki Zep, Cer, Zvornik, you could intercept conversations going in that direction but not -- and then you said from Zvornik, Gucevo, Cer and further on. That seems to be the opposite direction. You could not intercept those because we are talking about two different frequencies. What I do not understand yet is that if the terrain doesn't oppose intercepting those conversations, how the frequencies, if you have the equipment to listen in to two different frequencies, why couldn't you intercept those radio signals with technical equipment which could intercept on more than one frequency? Could you explain to us this obstruction to intercept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we talk about the direction of radiation from Zvornik towards Gucevo and from Gucevo towards Cer, it is guided radiation. The relay connection has guided, directed radiation. So that from any of these places Zvornik, Gucevo, Cer, if we talk about radiation from these parts, none of them are directed at Muslim territory. This beaming is not directed at Muslim territory. So I claim that this direction is impossible to intercept. From Zvornik towards Gucevo and Cer is different from the opposite direction because it's broadcast on one frequency. Whatever is broadcast towards Zvornik can be intercepted. I never disputed that. But from Zvornik towards Gucevo and Cer, it's not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in this last answer you introduce both direction of the beam and frequency. Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both are important. One goes with the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I now do understand that you say if you transmit in one direction, that if behind the target or on its way to the reception station, if there are Muslim forces, they can intercept; whereas you said that was not the case in one direction but it was the case in the other direction. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We take a break, and we'll resume in 20 minutes from now, at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to verify whether the videolink is still functioning properly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I can confirm that we can see and we can hear you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The same is true for this side. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, on paragraph 22 of your statement, which is D878, you said: "Some of the communication lines were not safe." And you would agree with me some of your RRU-800 lines were not safe, meaning they could and were intercepted at times by the enemy; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you had just told us that -- on temporary transcript page 16, that there was no need to make any frequency changes but that you also said that you and the Main Staff had the authority and the ability to make changes if needed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that I and the Main Staff had authority to change them. I said we did not have the authority to change them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say, and I quote: "The chief of communications of the Main Staff and I, as the chief of the communications of the Drina Corps, were in a position to change frequencies. However, our devices were directed towards the devices of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which means that we would have been automatically cut off." So let me -- I apologise for saying "authority." I should have said you could have changed the frequencies had you so desired; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: We could change the frequencies had we wanted to, but then our connections would have been cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's because your communications relied on going through Gucevo and Cer, which was in Serbia, and unless you coordinated the frequency change with Serbia, you would be cut off; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you did communicate with your colleagues in the radio relay station at Cer, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was not in contact with the colleague at Cer. I was in contact with the colleague at Gucevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me remind you of something you said in the Popovic case. It's at e-court pages 60 and 61 at the transcript of the Popovic case 22320, line 24. And you said: "... I mentioned that when there were interruptions, the operators could change the frequency, but they were duty-bound to inform and update everybody concerned. They could do that in case they suspected interferences or that they were being listened in." So not only did you have the ability to change the frequencies as well as the Main Staff, but these operators also could change the frequency, your own operators could change the frequencies. Do you stand by that statement you made in Popovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do. These operators could change the frequencies but you correctly stated in what circumstances. And simultaneously they had to inform me, because I was in charge of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've testified today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Witness, the answer you are giving now seems to be a bit of the opposite, because you earlier said if you would change frequencies, the system would collapse. And you now say you could change the frequencies, though you had inform other partners in the whole trajectory. Now, these answers make me urge you to tell us not only one possibility, that is, that the system would collapse; but also that the change of frequencies could be effected, could be made by informing your counterparts in the whole system so that it would not collapse. So could you please give us the full information if questions are asked. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, did you mean - when you mentioned the collapse - that that would only collapse if you didn't co-ordinate that frequency change with your Serbian colleagues at Gucevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. One radio relay route between two participants. Let's say, for example, Zvornik-Gucevo. In certain situations of interference or impossibility of quality communication on that route, the participants could, in agreement, simultaneously change the frequency and inform thereof along the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And they could do that not just because of weather interference. They could do that if they received jamming from the enemy too; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you've now -- you've also said in your statement and you've testified to that there was no need throughout the war to change the frequencies. But you don't really mean that, do you, Colonel? With bad weather and jamming, frequencies were changed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said whatever I meant. I still mean the same thing, and I'm saying it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, hang on to your -- your document D879, where you list 14 frequencies for the RRU-800, and perhaps the diagram. We'll be getting back to that a bit, but I would like to ask you a couple of other areas. And you were an officer in the Drina Corps in July 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember what date you were actually the duty officer at the Drina Corps in July?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember I was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 05789.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, what you should be seeing is something we've picked up from the -- what we call the Drina Corps archives and is a duty officers' list for July. We believe this is 1995. And if you -- we can blow up your side, we see your name at number 14. And if we go across this document and we look in at the black filled-in square, we see that it's filled in under 13. Does that mean you were the duty officer on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you recall the date that General Mladic came by the Vlasenica headquarters when you were on duty on the 13th of July? You may recall he promoted General Krstic to be the commander of the corps and retired General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that, but whether it was on the 13th when I was on duty or a day before or a day later, I'm not sure. But I was present when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were present when what happened?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When Colonel Krstic was appointed corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe what Mladic did. Was there a ceremony of sorts? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: We were lined up in the corridor at the corps command, and General Mladic said: From this day on, the corps commander is Colonel Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who was lined up?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: About ten of us who worked at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who do you remember in particular? Was Krstic there?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There was General Mladic. I think Krstic was there too, but General Mladic and General Zivanovic were there for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly what time of day did this take place? For example, was it dark or light outside?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was about 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long had Mladic been at the Drina Corps headquarters before this little lining-up ceremony at 7.00 or 8.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how long he had been at the corps command. This lining up and transition of duty of the corps commander lasted about 15 minutes. Now, how long after that Mladic stayed on, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall him coming into the duty office and getting on to the communications devices to call people? Did you help put him in touch with people?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had let this go for some time but now I think I do have to rise to object. We've been going approximately 15 minutes with topics that are neither arising from the statement nor the direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the rules have been rather appropriately flexible on that and this is something this witness has known about and has talked about before. And this has to do with General Mladic and his time and whereabouts, a pretty important topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Questions relating to the support of the Prosecution's case are allowed in cross-examination. The witness apparently has knowledge about these events which the Prosecution considers relevant. Therefore, Mr. McCloskey may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, my last question was: Do you recall him coming by the duty office and communicating with -- with anyone?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he could have communicated, if he'd wanted to, with people in Pale, like President Karadzic, couldn't he have, over your radio system?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: With our communications, he could get in touch with anyone he wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what would the route be from the Drina Corps headquarters in Vlasenica to Pale? I can take you probably as far as Vlasenica, Veliki Zep. Then where?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: From Veliki Zep, I think it went to Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's right near Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And briefly, just lastly on this document, the duty officers' book, do you recognise number 3 there as Ignjat Milanovic? That was an officer you worked for. We have him as the chief of the anti-aircraft defence. You know him?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew him. He died about ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And number 12, Lieutenant-Colonel Rajko Krsmanovic. Did you know him and work with him?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew him, and I still know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And according to this document, he would have been duty officer on the 18th of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05789 receives Exhibit Number P7055, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. McCloskey, if you ask the witness whether the document tells us that, then we can read that, we can see that as well. If you expect the witness to have any personal knowledge about it, then, of course, you should ask him about it, whether he has any recollection about that date and that person being on duty. But you asked about whether the document tells us that. The Chamber can read. We leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed -- could I ask one question for the witness. Witness, we just looked at that document which was the list of duty officers. Now, first of all, some of the boxes are blackened. Does that mean that only on those dates you were present or was it that you had a specific duty on those dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During those days, we were assigned to be duty operations officers at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it doesn't mean that on other dates you would not have been present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Right, that it does not mean that you were not present. So you could have been present on other dates as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did I offer that into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was already entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Your Honour. [Microphone not activated]. Could we go to another document, 65 ter 04106.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you'll see that this is a document with a signature we believe is Radenko Jovicic. And as you can see, it's entitled: The hand-over of the corps commander duties, and it's dated 13 July. And we see that it talks about General Mladic in the first paragraph and the hand-over. Would this be the time that you were talking about when -- that the hand-over duties were taken?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This document says so unequivocally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if can you help us, we see this stamp at the bottom, and we see that it's received at 2000 hours and processed at 2035, and does that tell you that this ceremony where General Mladic promoted Krstic to the commander occurred before this time? I'm guess I'm saying that the announcement that he had become the commander would not have happened until after the ceremony where he was made commander. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a fact the appointment and the transition of duties was around 7.00. Then this document was drafted and sent to the communications centre to be forwarded according to that list that you see next to this stamp on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04106 receives Exhibit Number P7056, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to 65 ter 06073.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you may remember this document from the Popovic case, but as you'll see it's -- soon, that it's dated 22 April 1993, that same year that your frequency document, D879, came out. And if you take a look at it, you'll see in that first paragraph, the chief of intelligence for the Zvornik Brigade, Drago Nikolic is reporting that: "We have a confirmation that the enemy is intensively intercepting our radio and radio relay communications and particularly active are their interception centres in Tuzla and Trovrh (Gorazde)." Do you have any reason to disagree with Drago Nikolic's assessment here?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There's no reason for me to disagree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we look near the bottom of this document, we see that he is recommending: Change often the frequencies and call-signs. He doesn't refer to whether it's the radio relay devices or to the -- the radio devices, the RUP devices you've talked about. So he means both, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06073 receives Exhibit Number P7057, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter 013138.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just 13138. I thought I had too many digits. And if we can look at the bottom of the page in the Serbian -- actually, the next -- the next -- well, we can see that this is from the Main Staff. Let's see who it's from. Can we go to the next page. All right. So we see it's General Mladic. Now let's go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now we've jumped from 1993 to 17 June 1995, and I won't spend much time with this, but you'll see that on the second paragraph, Mladic says: "According to the information available, the enemy is persistently and very effectively using secret military information obtained by intercepting our radio, radio relay, and PTT ... communications." So you agree with Mladic that this was the situation in 17 June 1995?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 13138 receives Exhibit Number P7058, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 24892.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'll see this is a document from the command of the Drina Corps, the -- Lieutenant-Colonel Vujadin Popovic, who we all know. It looks like it's sent out to most of the brigades and units of the Drina Corps. And that first paragraph states: "Through reconnaissance on the enemy's radio communications and information transmitted via radio, we've obtained information that our units are extremely careless when using communications equipment and do not verify the cryptographic data protection value of communications equipment." I won't read all the rest. We can see in the last paragraph he's talking about there should be more frequent changes, working frequencies and call-signs. So do you have any reason to object to or disagree with these observations of Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the chief of security in the corps command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please switch off all unnecessary microphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no reason for me not to agree with what he wrote. As the chief of communications, I carried out measures and procedures to deal with such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that you were being intensively intercepted in June of 1995. And not only that, but the habits of the radio -- of the radio operators and the people using the radios were sloppy, according to Colonel Popovic; correct? He used the words "extremely careless."

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Such things happened as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that could amount to things like not making sure the voice encryptor machine was properly working, not turning the key on the RUP-12 to make sure it's working, and other such things. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there seems to be a little bit of a problem with the videolink connection. Could we verify whether the other side of the videolink is able to hear and see us? It looks as if it's gone down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps the Defence would agree with me that this is a result of a radio disturbance in the radio waves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Actually, no, because they're fibre-optic cables, which is different technology, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think there are some radio towers that are running the fibre optics with -- but we can argue about that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber wonders what the relevance is of the reasons for this disruption for this case apart from that we can't hear and see anything. But it has been restored, I do understand. I now see again at the far end at least a picture, but I also see a microphone crossed-out symbol. Could we check both whether we can see you and whether we can hear you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I confirm that we can see you and we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the quality of the sound is -- that may be a matter of microphones rather than anything else. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, can you give me a couple of examples of the problems that Popovic is talking about, the carelessness.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The problems of carelessness lie in the fact that people were talking about operations, attacks, defence operations, transport of troops along certain roads in open microphone, as it were, through radio or relay communications. Code-names of units would be mentioned as well as their intentions or goals of their missions, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that include sometimes making mistakes regarding the use of encryption devices where they wouldn't turn them on properly or would not recognise they weren't working?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please switch off your microphone. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it comes to mistakes regarding the use of encryption devices, as far as I know, in the Drina Corps there were no such mistakes made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Never? During the entire war? Some private didn't turn the key on on his RUP-12 and --

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the entire war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to your -- it's D879. It's your 2 October document, 1993, that you send up to the corps with a list of frequencies for radio relay routes in use in the Drina Corps. And on paragraph 25 of your statement, which is D878, you say that: "I have been shown a document of the Drina Corps command of 2 October and I recognise this document as mine. In regard to this document, I can say briefly that the enemy was not able to intercept conversations outside the frequency ranges listed in this document." You have 14 frequencies listed in this document. Seven transmitting; seven receiving. Are you saying that the enemy was not able to intercept conversations other than these 14 frequencies?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, sir, are all the frequencies in use by the VRS in the Drina Corps's zone of responsibility noted in this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: All the frequencies in use by the VRS, they are not all specified in this document. Veliki Zep was -- and the Main Staff were in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, sir, if not all the frequencies used by the VRS in this document, you cannot conclude that the enemy was not able to intercept conversations outside the frequency range listed in this document?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. One second, please. We did not receive interpretation. Could the witness re-start his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can talk about the frequencies for which I was responsible as the chief of communications of the Drina Corps. I can't talk about other frequencies because I was not familiar with them. I don't know what their directions were. I don't have information about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So then your statement cannot be correct, where you say that the enemy was not able to intercept conversations outside the frequency ranges listed in this document.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This document of mine refers to the radio relay frequencies of the Drina Corps for which I was responsible. I stand by what I stated, and I can reinstate that firmly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could we see whether there's any confusion. Witness, did you intend to say that the enemy was unable to intercept any of the communication which went through the frequency as listed in this document, or did you intend to say that the enemy was unable to intercept any communication through frequencies which are not mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The letter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking on behalf of the chief of communications of the Drina Corps, and I take responsibility for the radio frequencies in that document. Anything that was collected beyond these frequencies, and I'm talking about the Drina Corps units, what I'm claiming is that that was not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's still a bit unclear to me. Do you mean to say that it was impossible that other frequencies were used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Units of the Drina Corps used the frequencies found in the document that I myself sent to the chief of the Main Staff. The units of the Drina Corps did not use any other frequencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There were frequencies not listed in your document -- no, let me ask it this way. You've already acknowledged that the enemy could intercept between Gucevo and Cer. What was the frequency between Gucevo and Cer?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Between Gucevo and Cer, I don't know what the frequency was. Even the chief of communications of the Main Staff didn't know that because that was not in our area of responsibility. Gucevo and Cer were in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So my point now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can get just one question out of this area, it might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My point, Colonel, now is the frequency between Gucevo and Cer is interceptable, as you say it is, and it is not one of the frequencies listed in your document. Therefore, you cannot say that the Muslims couldn't intercept conversations outside the frequency ranges. Gucevo-Cer is outside the frequency ranges and you've acknowledged they can intercept that. So your statement is not correct in paragraph 25; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We can --

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: For the following reason: I am speaking about the units and territory of the Drina Corps and the frequencies that they used there. When we're talking about Cer-Gucevo route, that was used for our communications as well. I agree with you in that respect, but only for the Cer-Gucevo direction. And the Gucevo-Zvornik direction. But nothing of that kind could happen in the opposite direction, absolutely impossible. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so, finally, you've made my point. You said there's an exception to your statement in 25, that there is a frequency outside the range in your document that they can intercept on. So we agree on that; correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with that. Only partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe that's good enough for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break. Could you give us an indication, Mr. McCloskey, how much more time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I certainly won't be asking to go over the two hours, but I hope to make this slightly more clear in the next 40 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're aware that the witness is limited in time. He cannot stay any longer than 2.00. But, therefore, even if we take a break now, then we should be well within that time for you to finish. Mr. Ivetic, as far as matters stand now, and I am aware that we're only halfway in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifteen minutes. Let's try to do our utmost best to see whether we can conclude the testimony of this witness by 2.00. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to put on the record that the videolink is not functioning in every respect perfectly, especially the view the other side of the videolink has on the one speaking here in The Hague may not be continuous and be interrupted now and then. Could I invite Madam Registrar at the other side of the videolink to immediately report if this technical problem reaches such levels that it disturbs the communication in such a way that we should reconsider to continue, yes or no. I also do understand that at least the audio is impeccable. Therefore, our interpreters can hear what is said on the other side and can interpret what we are saying. And I suggest to the parties that we live with this small inconvenience and continue. And, Mr. McCloskey, it's for you to do so. Mr. Mladic is apparently busy in showing the content of books to security where there is no need. If there's anything relevant in those books, then it is for counsel to bring it to the attention of the Chamber. Let's move on. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel Blagojevic, are you with us? All right, Colonel, can you hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I hear you. I hear you fine. Now, I want to take a short detour but I will get back to the radio routes, but I want to ask you about some officers and soldiers you may have worked with. We've gone over a bit on the duty officer roster, but the -- you've mentioned the Main Staff. And did you -- were you familiar with Radomir Prole? And who was he?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: We kept the list of duty officers at the Drina Corps, whereas Radomir Prole was the chief of communications for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you work with some officers and soldiers from the 67th Communications Regiment which was attached to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you knew a Lieutenant-Colonel Nedeljko Gredo, the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was also a colonel, Nedeljko Gredo; I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about a Milisav Radakovic at the 67th? I have him as a major but you may have known him as a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Milisav Radakovic. Yes, he was a colonel, major, later lieutenant-colonel. At that time he was deputy chief of communications for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about a -- I have him as a captain, Tihomir Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A Goran Zobic.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew Goran Zobic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was his job?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Zobic was the commander of the communications battalion in the communications regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the 67th?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about a code clerk - in your language a "sifrer" - named Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know him. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't remember Tomo Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about Dragan Acamovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mirko Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mirko Petrovic. Both the name and surname are very common in our parts. I knew one Mirko Petrovic who worked at the corps command with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was his job?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a commanding officer, komandir, in the communications section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was the name of that communications section?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was in the communications battalion, in the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you surely know of the 4th Radio Recon Platoon, the folks that did intercepting for you and the Drina Corps? Mirko Petrovic would send out reports regarding what they had intercepted to the corps. The 4th Radio Recon Platoon.

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mirko was the komandir of that platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So he wasn't what you had originally testified in the comms, he was the commander of this special intercept unit, the 4th Radio Recon Platoon?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you just reminded me. I had forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to your October 2nd document. It's D879. It's the one where you have the 14 frequencies written down. You have already acknowledged there is a frequency you don't know that goes from Gucevo to Cer. Now, let me ask you: What was the frequency between Veliki Zep and Jahorina, as you said, was the route to Pale?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that frequency either because it was the responsibility of the chief of communications of the Main Staff, Prole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's another frequency that is not listed in your document of 2 October 1993? Do you agree with me, it's not there?

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact --

utterances.speaker: NEDO BLAGOJEVIC
